n: Isaiah 6 records Isaiah’s call. In the year King Uzziah died (around 740 BC), Isaiah saw the Lord on a lofty throne, His robe filling the temple. Nephi says Isaiah saw his Redeemer; John 12:41 also says Isaiah saw Christ’s glory.

f.g: The trailing hem of his robe.

n: Seraphim — heavenly beings whose name means “burning ones” — stand above Him. With two wings they cover their faces in reverence, with two their feet in humility, and with two they fly.

f.g: Hebrew “burning ones” — angelic beings in God’s presence.

n: They call to each other: “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of Hosts.” Repeating a word three times is Hebrew’s strongest way to say “most holy.” His glory fills the whole earth.
The doorposts shake at their voice, and the temple fills with smoke — signs of God’s presence, as at Sinai.

f.w: the house was filled with smoke

n: Isaiah cries “Woe is me! I am undone!” Seeing God’s holiness makes him painfully aware of his own impurity and his people’s.
A seraph flies to him holding a live coal taken with tongs from the altar.

f.g: A glowing coal from the temple altar — a symbol of cleansing fire.

n: The seraph touches Isaiah’s lips with the coal: his guilt is removed and his sin purged. Cleansing comes from the altar of sacrifice — a symbol pointing to Christ’s Atonement.
The Lord asks, “Whom shall I send?” Isaiah answers, “Here am I; send me.” The same words recall Christ’s offer in the premortal council.
Isaiah’s message will be rejected. The KJV reads as a command (“understand not”); the Book of Mormon reads “they understood not,” describing the people’s own refusal to understand.
Isaiah’s preaching will make the people’s hearts “fat” (insensitive), their ears dull, and their eyes shut, because they refuse it. Truth rejected hardens the heart.

f.w: Make the heart of this people fat
f.g: Dull, unresponsive — Hebrew idiom for insensitivity.

n: “How long, Lord?” Until the cities are empty and the land desolate — fulfilled through the Assyrian and Babylonian invasions.
The Lord will remove the people far away, leaving the land abandoned — exile.
Yet a tenth will remain. Like a felled terebinth or oak that still has life in its stump, a “holy seed” will survive and grow again — the remnant of Israel.

f.g: The terebinth, a large tree that can resprout from its stump.
